input.strategy_title: Make RHOAI more usable for enterprise teams
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Several strategic accounts have told field teams that RHOAI "feels hard to use
at enterprise scale". Feedback arrived through different channels and has not
been consolidated; the quotes below are representative but partially
contradictory. Leadership wants visible usability progress this release.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | — | Administration should be simpler. One account wants fewer configuration options exposed ("too many knobs"), another explicitly wants more fine-grained controls per project. |
| HLR-2 | — | Onboarding a new data scientist should take "less than a day". It is not defined what onboarding includes or where the day is currently spent. |
| HLR-3 | — | The platform should "integrate better" with existing enterprise tooling. No specific tools were named in the consolidated feedback. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Publish a whitepaper describing enterprise usability best practices on RHOAI. |

## Affected Components

- Dashboard
- Notebooks

## Out of Scope

Nothing has been explicitly scoped out.

## Open Questions

1. Which accounts' feedback takes precedence when requirements conflict (HLR-1)?
2. What does "onboarding" cover for HLR-2 — cluster access, project setup,
   first workbench, or first deployed model?
3. Which enterprise tools does HLR-3 actually mean?

# Simplify Dashboard administration configuration (direction A)

## Description

Implements the "simplify" outcome of the administration-usability direction
decision: reduce and consolidate the configuration options exposed to
administrators in the RHOAI Dashboard, backing the removed knobs with sane
defaults, so that common administration tasks require fewer decisions. This
epic exists only if the direction decision selects simplification (outcome A
or a layered outcome that includes it).

## Scope

- Reduce the set of administration options exposed in the Dashboard per the
  direction decision document, concentrating on the surfaces the decision
  identifies.
- Provide sane defaults for every option that is no longer exposed, so
  existing behavior remains correct without administrator action.
- Keep an escape hatch for power users where the decision calls for one
  (advanced/hidden configuration), per the direction decision.
- Update in-product administration guidance affected by the changed surfaces.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The administration options exposed in the Dashboard match the reduced set
  defined by the direction decision.
- Every removed option has a documented default, and workflows that relied on
  the removed knobs behave correctly with that default.
- The change is reversible: a feature flag or configuration restore path
  exists to re-expose removed options, and a rollback plan is documented
  (this epic replaces an existing administration surface).
- Existing Dashboard functionality is unaffected by regression.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 — implements the "fewer configuration options exposed" reading of the
  administration-usability requirement.

# Fine-grained per-project administration controls (direction B)

## Description

Implements the "fine-grained controls" outcome of the administration-usability
direction decision: add per-project granularity to administrative controls in
the RHOAI Dashboard, so administrators of individual projects can tune their
own settings instead of working from platform-wide configuration only. This
epic exists only if the direction decision selects per-project controls
(outcome B or a layered outcome that includes them).

## Scope

- Add per-project administrative control capability to the Dashboard for the
  surfaces identified by the direction decision document.
- Build on the existing project-scoped model: the Dashboard authenticates via
  OpenShift OAuth with project-scoped RBAC, and platform-wide defaults are
  administered through the OdhDashboardConfig CR — per-project settings must
  compose with both.
- Define override semantics: a project-level setting overrides the
  platform-wide default where the direction decision allows it.
- Update administration guidance for the new per-project controls.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Administrators can configure the identified controls at per-project
  granularity through the Dashboard.
- Per-project settings compose correctly with OpenShift OAuth project-scoped
  RBAC — users cannot alter controls for projects they do not administer.
- Projects without overrides behave exactly as before (platform-wide defaults
  unchanged).
- Existing administration workflows are unaffected by regression.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 — implements the "more fine-grained controls per project" reading of
  the administration-usability requirement.

# Resolve conflicting administration-usability direction for enterprise accounts

## Description

HLR-1 asks that "administration should be simpler", but the consolidated
account feedback is directly contradictory: one strategic account wants fewer
configuration options exposed ("too many knobs"), while another explicitly
wants more fine-grained controls per project. This investigation consolidates
the feedback behind HLR-1, determines which direction (or combination) takes
precedence, and records a decision that gates all administration-usability
implementation work on the Dashboard.

## Scope

- Consolidate the enterprise account feedback behind HLR-1: sources, quotes,
  and the weight each account carries.
- Inventory the current administration/configuration surface of the Dashboard
  as context — per-component feature flags and defaults are administered
  through the OdhDashboardConfig CR today.
- Decide the direction for administration usability. The bounded outcomes are:
  - **A — Simplify**: reduce and consolidate the configuration options exposed
    to administrators, backing them with sane defaults.
  - **B — Fine-grained controls**: add per-project administrative control
    granularity.
  - **Layered**: simplified defaults for the common path plus advanced
    per-project controls (both outcomes apply).
- Record the decision (ADR or equivalent decision document) with rationale,
  the affected administration surfaces, and the selected outcome label.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A consolidated feedback summary exists that names the conflicting
  requirements, their account sources, and the precedence rule applied.
- A decision document records the selected outcome (A, B, or layered) with
  rationale and identifies which Dashboard administration surfaces are
  affected.
- The decision is agreed by the stakeholders who own the conflicting account
  relationships.
- The outcome is recorded in one of the bounded labels so the corresponding
  implementation work can be planned immediately.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 — resolves the contradictory administration-usability feedback and
  determines which implementation direction is pursued.

# Define data-scientist onboarding scope and time baseline

## Description

HLR-2 requires that onboarding a new data scientist take "less than a day",
but the strategy does not define what onboarding includes or where the day is
currently spent. This investigation defines the onboarding scope, baselines
the current time-to-onboard, and identifies the friction points — the output
determines what onboarding implementation work exists and where it lands.

## Scope

- Define what "onboarding a new data scientist" covers. Candidate stages named
  in the strategy: cluster access, project setup, first workbench, first
  deployed model. Determine which are in scope and in what order.
- Baseline the current onboarding journey: where elapsed time and friction
  actually occur today for each in-scope stage (Dashboard-side project
  creation and workbench spawn, Notebooks-side workbench lifecycle and image
  readiness, and any environment/access steps).
- Produce a prioritized list of friction points with the responsible surface
  (Dashboard vs. Notebooks vs. out of product scope).
- Record the scope decision so downstream implementation work can be planned;
  explicitly call out whether the workbench experience is in scope.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The onboarding scope is defined: which candidate stages are included, with
  a stated rationale.
- A current-state baseline exists showing where time is spent across the
  in-scope stages.
- Friction points are identified, prioritized, and mapped to the surface that
  owns each.
- The scope decision explicitly states whether Notebooks-side workbench work
  is included, since that determines whether a Notebooks implementation epic
  exists.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 — converts the undefined "onboarding in less than a day" requirement
  into a defined scope and baseline that implementation work can target.

# Identify target enterprise tools for integration

## Description

HLR-3 asks that the platform "integrate better" with existing enterprise
tooling, but the consolidated feedback names no specific tools. This
investigation identifies which enterprise tools the strategic accounts
actually mean, prioritizes them, and determines what "integrate better"
concretely entails for each — the output determines the scope and approach of
all downstream integration work.

## Scope

- Go back to the feedback sources (field teams and the strategic accounts
  behind the consolidated feedback) and extract the specific enterprise tools
  implied by "integrate better" — e.g. identity/auth providers, source
  control, monitoring, ticketing, data platforms.
- For each named tool, capture what the account expects from the integration
  (user-facing surface vs. platform-level behavior).
- Prioritize the tool list by account impact and feasibility, and confirm the
  priority with stakeholders.
- Record the outcome: a prioritized, validated tool list with expected
  integration surfaces, or an explicit finding that no actionable tooling
  requirement exists (in which case HLR-3 is closed as not actionable).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A consolidated list of specific enterprise tools is produced from the
  account feedback, with the expecting account named for each.
- Each listed tool has a stated integration expectation and a candidate
  integration surface in the platform.
- The list is prioritized and validated with the stakeholders who own the
  account relationships.
- The investigation closes with either an actionable tool list or an explicit
  not-actionable finding — it does not end with an open question.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 — converts the unspecified "integrate better with enterprise tooling"
  requirement into a concrete, prioritized tool list that implementation work
  can target.

# Dashboard onboarding experience for new data scientists

## Description

Implements the Dashboard-side improvements of the defined data-scientist
onboarding scope, so that a new data scientist can complete the in-scope
onboarding stages through the Dashboard within the time target set by the
"less than a day" requirement. The Dashboard owns the user-facing console for
data science projects and workbench creation, so any product-UI onboarding
step lands here. The concrete scope is determined by the onboarding scope
definition and its friction baseline.

## Scope

- Improve the Dashboard surfaces the defined onboarding scope touches —
  project creation, workbench spawning, and any guided/first-run experience
  the scope decision calls for.
- Address the Dashboard-side friction points identified in the onboarding
  baseline, in priority order.
- Keep scope strictly consistent with the defined onboarding scope; anything
  the scope decision excludes is out of scope here.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A new data scientist can complete every in-scope onboarding stage that has a
  Dashboard surface, end to end, through the Dashboard.
- The Dashboard-side steps identified in the friction baseline are addressed
  or explicitly dispositioned.
- The measured time for the Dashboard-side portion of onboarding supports the
  overall "less than a day" target for the defined scope.
- Existing project and workbench management functionality is unaffected by
  regression.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 — delivers the Dashboard-side portion of onboarding a new data
  scientist in less than a day.

# Notebooks workbench onboarding experience

## Description

Implements the Notebooks-side improvements of the defined data-scientist
onboarding scope: getting a new data scientist from workbench spawn to a
usable first workbench quickly. The Notebooks component owns the workbench
(notebook server) lifecycle — the controller reconciles Notebook CRs into
StatefulSets with OAuth sidecars, including workbench image readiness and the
idle culler. This epic exists only if the defined onboarding scope includes
the workbench experience.

## Scope

- Address Notebooks-side friction identified in the onboarding baseline for
  the first-workbench journey, in priority order (e.g. time from workbench
  spawn to usable state, image selection and readiness behavior).
- Preserve existing workbench lifecycle behavior: culling defaults and
  per-workbench overrides continue to be administered through the Dashboard,
  and OAuth sidecar behavior is unchanged.
- Keep scope strictly consistent with the defined onboarding scope.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A new data scientist's first workbench reaches a usable state within the
  expectation set by the defined onboarding scope.
- The Notebooks-side friction points identified in the onboarding baseline
  are addressed or explicitly dispositioned.
- Existing workbench lifecycle behavior (culling, OAuth sidecars, per-workbench
  overrides) is unaffected by regression.
- If the defined onboarding scope does not include the workbench experience,
  this epic is removed rather than forced — that outcome is recorded by the
  scope definition, not here.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 — delivers the Notebooks-side portion of onboarding a new data
  scientist in less than a day.
